notes: COI flag: an author named Jun Wang is present (third author, Department of Mechanical Engineering, Santa Clara University, per the article byline and Crossref; OpenAlex lists the name as 'Jun Liang Wang'). The same name is on P00428, whose prefill records an advisor co-author; Mark Fuge co-authors both. Codes checked in the closed-list order. FT-DUPLICATE: the conference paper P01929 ('... for 2D Heat Sink Design', IDETC-CIE 2024) is in the pool but not coded. Sec. 1 says this article expands it (ref. [25]) with a reworked public codebase, re-run experiments and extra analysis. The journal version of record is open access and more complete, so P01900 is the primary version; if the verifier treats the two as one study, P01929 is the duplicate. FT-SCOPE and FT-TYPE do not apply (density-based TO with generative models; research article). FT-DOMAIN applies: the MTO problem couples the steady incompressible Navier-Stokes equations with an energy balance (Sec. 3.1, Eq. 1; App. A, Eqs. A2-A3), solved with an OpenFOAM-based solver (Yu et al., ref. [57]) with Brinkman-type inverse permeability and RAMP interpolation (Eq. A4). The design variable separates solid and fluid, and fluid power dissipation is a constraint and a second objective. This is fluid-flow TO (conjugate heat transfer), which PROTOCOL §4 excludes; §3.1 admits heat conduction only. Would-be coding if the verifier overrules FT-DOMAIN: the abstract compares only ML models (VQGAN vs a continuous autoencoder; transformer vs WGAN-GP). The conclusion claims, qualitatively, substantially lower wall-clock time and compute than repeatedly solving the full MTO problem. The first quantitative classical comparison is Table 3 (Sec. 4.4; means over 5 seeds, about 1100 designs per model), which compares the transformer designs after a 20-step MTO warm start with the cold-start MTO test set: 1-PDA_s 0.317-0.330 vs 0.402 (lower is better), mean power dissipation 39.29-41.52 vs 46.50, mean temperature 15.53-15.72 vs 14.99 (test set better), valid designs 79.51-86.84% vs 91.68%. That gives stratum Q. Every generated design is post-processed by the 20-step MTO warm start (Sec. 4.4; App. E, which says rounding alone gives similar benefits), so a time comparison would have to count it (R1 post-processing clause). Validity is checked by the MTO solver after warm start (Table 3 note). Minor inconsistency: the text gives the test set's mean temperature as 14.97, Table 3 as 14.99. C3 facts: the dataset came from 10,000 design-condition sets run on an HPC cluster (the first 5,000 by Latin hypercube sampling), of which 5,666 converged without constraint violation (Sec. 3.1); generation time is not stated in the main text. VQGAN Stage 1 trains in under 2 h for 100 epochs on one NVIDIA H100 (Sec. 3.2.1, item 4); the transformer trains for up to 500 epochs (Sec. 4.3). Code (github.com/IDEALLab/VQGAN-TO) and data (huggingface.co/datasets/IDEALLab/MTO-2D) are linked in footnotes 2-3 and the data availability statement; neither was checked. Screening code was I-UNCLEAR. Decision order positions: P01900 123, P01929 315 (audit/screening/pilot_final_order.csv); the two records carry different titles, DOIs and venues, so they are not the same version and the §11 duplicate tie-break does not apply.

decision.reason: The optimized device is a heat sink whose density field separates solid from fluid, under steady incompressible Navier-Stokes and convective energy equations solved in OpenFOAM, with fluid power dissipation as constraint and objective (Sec. 3.1, Eq. 1, p. 101704-3; App. A, Eqs. A2-A3, p. 101704-14). That is fluid-flow TO, which PROTOCOL §4 excludes; §3.1 admits heat conduction only.
